summary:
I've been overhauling BudgetTracker, mostly under the hood. The biggest change was moving the database off a shared SQL Server instance onto Postgres on Supabase and rewriting the data layer with Drizzle from scratch — no compatibility shim, since being single-user gave me a window for breaking changes. That meant migrating 8,239 transactions and 773 merchants in a single cut, right before the switchover. One gotcha along the way: the Supabase session pooler requires TLS but its certificate isn't signed by a default CA, so strict verify throws and no-SSL throws; the only thing that connects is `no-verify`. It's documented, but you only find it by failing both ways first.

The in-app AI assistant got rebuilt at the same time. It now supports multiple providers — Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, or a local model — with per-user API keys stored encrypted. The interesting part was the tool-calling loop: the model can request account balances, transaction lists, and date-range summaries by calling read-only functions, with `userId` injected server-side so it never touches auth logic directly. One concrete fix: the local model was burning its reasoning budget on chain-of-thought and returning empty answers, so tool-heavy calls now disable thinking mode while conversational turns keep it on.

I also built a small MCP server into BudgetTracker so Hermes-Agent — my local AI agent — can ask financial questions against it. Eleven read-only tools, each gated by scopes modeled on GitHub fine-grained PATs: each API key declares what it can read, and tools only advertise themselves to keys that have permission. One rule throughout: all the math lives in SQL. Anomaly detection runs a z-score over category spend history; cash flow projection walks a ledger forward applying scheduled income and expense rules. The model gets numbers, it doesn't compute them. Getting the two services talking required tracking down a silent 401: BudgetTracker was signing webhook payloads Stripe-style (`t=timestamp,v1=hmac(timestamp.body)`) while Hermes-Agent expected a plain body HMAC with no timestamp in the signed string. Every real delivery failed until I added the second header.

Separately, I've been building an RSVP reader for Claude Code output — a tool that mirrors replies and flashes them one phrase at a time. The adaptive pacing layer uses a smaller model to score phrase density and return timing multipliers without touching the text itself. The web version holds the API credentials server-side and streams phrase events to the browser so the token never crosses to the client. Ninety-two tests so far, with a few planned features (per-user WPM calibration, conversation scrollback) not started yet.

highlights.oneLiner: Migrated DB to Postgres/Supabase + Drizzle, rebuilt AI assistant with multi-provider support and tool-calling loop
Wired BudgetTracker MCP (11 read-only tools, scoped api_keys) into Hermes; fixed BT→Hermes webhook 401 signature mismatch
Building Cadence RSVP speed-reader for Claude output with adaptive Haiku pacing and a web GUI
Watchlist UX batch deployed: searchable merchants, month-scoped drill-down, single CTA, back link
